Department A - Books, periodicals and newspapers
Department B - Games, toys and fancy goods.
The following balances were extracted from her nominal ledger on 31st March, 1993:
Sales - Department A N150,000 (Cr), Department B N100,000 (Cr); Stocks 1/4/92: Department A N2,500, Department B N2,000; Purchases: Department A N118,000, Department B N82,000; Wages of Sales Assistants: Department A N10,000, Department B N7,500; Newspaper delivery wages N1,500; General office salaries N7,500; Rates N1,300; Insurance N500; Electricity N1,200; Repairs to premises N250; Telephone N250; Cleaning N300; Accountancy and Audit fees N1,200; General office expenses N600.
Stocks 31/3/93: Department A N3,000; Department B N1,500.

You are required to prepare a Departmental Trading, Profit and Loss Account of Abike Amuludun for the year ended 31st March, 1993.
Note: Apportionment should be made using the following bases:
Area - Rates, insurance, electricity, repairs, telephone and cleaning.
Turnover - General office salaries, Accountancy and Audit fees, and general office expenses.

Audu, Bisi and Sam are in partnership sharing profits and losses in the ratio 2:2:1, respectively.
The partnership agreement provides:
(a) for payment of interest at 5% per annum on the credit balance of each partner's Capital and 15% on Current Account (credit balance) at the beginning of each year;
(b) that no interest on drawings be charged;
(c) for the payment of a salary of N2,500 per annum to Sam together with a 2% commission on the trading profit after charging current account interest, salary and the commission, but before charging interest on Capital.
The partners' balances as at 1st July, 1993 were as follows: Current Account - Audu N2,000 Cr., Bisi N200 Dr., Sam N400 Dr.; Capital Account - Audu N16,000, Bisi N12,000, Sam N4,000.
Drawings for the year were: Audu N5,200; Bisi N3,700; Sam N4,800.
The trading profit for the year ended 30th June, 1994 was N22,282.
You are required to prepare:
(i) the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account for the year ended 30th June, 1994;
(ii) the Current Account for each partner in columnar form, and
(iii) the Capital Account for each partner in columnar form.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Interest on current account: Audu only, 15% of 2,000 = N300; Sam's salary N2,500
3 marks: Commission: 2% x (22,282 - 300 - 2,500 - C) = C, giving C = N382
2 marks: Interest on capital at 5%: Audu 800, Bisi 600, Sam 200 (N1,600)
2 marks: Residual profit N17,500 shared 2:2:1: Audu 7,000, Bisi 7,000, Sam 3,500
4 marks: Current accounts c/d: Audu N4,900 Cr, Bisi N3,700 Cr, Sam N1,382 Cr
2 marks: Capital accounts unchanged: Audu 16,000, Bisi 12,000, Sam 4,000 balances c/d
questions.explanation: Appropriation: trading profit 22,282; less interest on current account (Audu 15% of 2,000) 300, Sam's salary 2,500, and commission 382 (2% of the profit after commission: 0.02 x 19,482 / 1.02); less interest on capital 800 + 600 + 200 = 1,600; residual 17,500 shared 2:2:1 as Audu 7,000, Bisi 7,000, Sam 3,500. Current accounts: Audu 2,000 + 300 + 800 + 7,000 - 5,200 = 4,900 Cr; Bisi -200 + 600 + 7,000 - 3,700 = 3,700 Cr; Sam -400 + 2,500 + 382 + 200 + 3,500 - 4,800 = 1,382 Cr. Capital accounts are unchanged at 16,000, 12,000 and 4,000 (balances b/d and c/d) since no interest on drawings or capital changes occurred.

questions.explanation: (a) Unpresented cheques, uncredited lodgements, bank charges, standing orders/direct debits, direct credits (e.g. dividends), dishonoured cheques, errors. (b) Unpresented cheques: entered in the cash book as payments but not yet presented to the bank, so the bank balance is higher. Uncredited lodgements: debited in the cash book but not yet credited by the bank, so the bank balance is lower. Bank charges and standing orders: deducted by the bank but not yet in the cash book, so the bank balance is lower. Direct credits such as dividends: credited by the bank but not yet recorded in the cash book, so the bank balance is higher. Dishonoured cheques: the bank reverses the credit while the cash book still shows it. Errors: wrong amounts or postings by either party distort one of the balances.

3 marks: (b)(i) the provision (or increase in it) is charged to profit and loss account; the provision is deducted from debtors in the balance sheet

questions.explanation: (a) Adjustments correct the ledger balances so that income and expenses relate to the period (accruals, prepayments, provisions, depreciation); closing entries transfer the adjusted nominal account balances to the trading and profit and loss account, leaving those accounts with nil balances. (b)(i) Debit profit and loss with the provision or its increase (credit for a decrease) and show debtors less the provision in the balance sheet. (ii) Deduct the prepayment from the expense charged and show it under current assets. (iii) Add accrued income to the income credited and show it as a current asset. (iv) Charge the year's depreciation to profit and loss account and show the asset at cost less accumulated depreciation.

(b) Give two similarities and two differences between a Receipt and Payment Account and an Income and Expenditure Account. [9 marks]

4 marks: (b) two similarities, 2 marks each: both prepared by not-for-profit organisations; both prepared at the end of the period/summarise the period's transactions
3 marks: (b) first difference well explained, e.g. R&P is a summary of the cash book while I&E is equivalent to the profit and loss account
2 marks: (b) second difference, e.g. R&P includes capital and revenue items on a cash basis while I&E includes revenue items only on an accruals basis; or R&P balance is cash/bank while I&E balance is a surplus or deficit
questions.explanation: (a) They are not set up to make profit; they exist to render services to members or society; their capital is called the accumulated fund; their income comes from subscriptions, donations and levies; an excess of income is a surplus, not a profit. (b) Similarities: both are prepared by clubs and societies, and both are prepared at the end of the financial period from the year's records. Differences: the Receipts and Payments Account is a summary of the cash book, while the Income and Expenditure Account is the club's profit and loss account. Receipts and Payments includes both capital and revenue items for the period on a cash basis; Income and Expenditure includes only revenue items on an accruals basis. The closing balance of Receipts and Payments is cash or bank, while that of Income and Expenditure is a surplus or deficit.

questions.stem:
(a) List four source documents used for making entries in a cash book. [4 marks]
(b) State four classifications of costs revealed by manufacturing account. [6 marks]
(c) State two reasons for the preparation of manufacturing accounts. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) any four, 1 mark each: receipts; cheque counterfoils/stubs; paying-in slips (deposit slips); bank statements; cash sales vouchers/tickets; payment vouchers
6 marks: (b) four classifications, 1.5 marks each: prime cost (direct costs); factory overheads (indirect manufacturing costs); work-in-progress adjustment; cost of production (total manufacturing cost); also direct materials and direct labour as components of prime cost
3 marks: (c) first reason: to ascertain the cost of goods produced/cost of production, for pricing decisions
2 marks: (c) second reason: to compare the cost of making goods with buying them; to control manufacturing costs; to separate manufacturing profit/costs from trading results
questions.explanation: (a) Receipts, cheque counterfoils, paying-in slips and bank statements (also cash sales tickets and payment vouchers). (b) A manufacturing account shows the prime cost (direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses), factory overheads (indirect costs such as factory rent, supervisors' salaries and depreciation of plant), the work-in-progress adjustment, and the cost of production of goods completed. (c) It is prepared to find the cost of production so that selling prices can be fixed, and to help management control costs and compare the cost of making goods with the cost of buying them.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem:
(a) What is a Trial Balance? [3 marks]
(b) State two purposes for preparing a trial balance. [4 marks]
(c) List and explain four errors that are not disclosed by a trial balance. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) a list of the debit and credit balances extracted from the ledger accounts on a particular date, to check the arithmetical accuracy of the double entry
4 marks: (b) two purposes, 2 marks each: to check arithmetical accuracy of the ledger postings; to provide a summary of balances for preparing final accounts; to help locate errors
8 marks: (c) four errors listed and explained, 2 marks each: omission (transaction not recorded at all); commission (correct amount posted to the wrong account of the same class); principle (posted to the wrong class of account, e.g. capital as revenue); original entry (wrong amount in the book of original entry); complete reversal of entries; compensating errors
questions.explanation: (a) A trial balance is a list of all the debit and credit balances extracted from the ledger on a given date to test the arithmetical accuracy of the double entry. (b) It checks that the double entry has been arithmetically correct, and it provides a summary of balances from which the final accounts are prepared. (c) Errors not revealed: omission (a transaction left out completely); commission (posted to the wrong personal account of the same class); principle (e.g. purchase of a fixed asset debited to purchases); original entry (the wrong amount entered in the day book and posted to both sides); complete reversal (debit and credit sides interchanged); and compensating errors (two errors that cancel each other out).

questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) customs/generally accepted practices that guide accountants in recording transactions and preparing financial statements
4 marks: (b)(i) materiality: only items significant enough to affect users' decisions need separate or strict treatment; trivial items may be treated in the simplest way
4 marks: (b)(ii) consistency: the same accounting methods should be applied from one period to another so that results are comparable; any change must be disclosed
4 marks: (b)(iii) conservatism (prudence): profits are not anticipated but all possible losses are provided for; assets are not overstated and liabilities not understated
questions.explanation: (a) Accounting conventions are generally accepted customs and practices that guide accountants in recording transactions and preparing financial statements. (b)(i) Materiality: only items large or significant enough to influence users need strict treatment. Small items, such as a cheap stapler, may be written off as expenses. (ii) Consistency: once a method (e.g. of depreciation or stock valuation) is adopted, it should be used from period to period so that results are comparable. Any change must be disclosed. (iii) Conservatism (prudence): do not anticipate profits, but provide for all foreseeable losses. Where there is a choice, choose the lower value for assets and the higher for liabilities.

questions.stem:
Salamata Njai's cash book on 28th February, 2006 showed a credit balance of D2,740 and his bank statement showed a balance of D1,600 overdrawn on the same date. On investigation, the following were revealed:
(a) A cheque issued to Jon Alfa amounting to D900 had not been presented to the bank for payment.
(b) A cheque of D820 from Hajia Fatou entered in the cash book as paid into the bank had not been credited by the bank.
(c) The receipts side of the cash book had been undercast by D440.
(d) Bank charges of D150 entered in the bank statement had not been entered in the cash book.
(e) A cheque for D1,100 drawn on the accounts had been charged by the bank in error to another account.
(f) A cheque for D200 paid into the bank had been dishonoured and shown as such by the bank but no entry was made in the cash book.
(g) A cheque drawn for D62 had been entered in the cash book in error as D26.
(h) A cheque for D94 drawn by another customer of the same name had been charged into Salamata Njai's bank account in error.
You are required to:
(i) show the appropriate adjustments to be made in the cash book; and
(ii) prepare a bank reconciliation statement as at 28th February, 2006.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Cash book: balance b/d (overdraft) D2,740 on the credit side
2 marks: Debit: undercast receipts D440
3 marks: Credit: bank charges D150, dishonoured cheque D200, understated cheque D36 (62 - 26)
2 marks: Adjusted cash book balance: overdraft D2,686
1 mark: Reconciliation: overdraft per bank statement D1,600
2 marks: Add unpresented cheque D900 and cheque wrongly charged to another account D1,100
2 marks: Less uncredited cheque D820 and cheque of another customer charged in error D94
2 marks: Overdraft per adjusted cash book D2,686
questions.explanation: Adjusted cash book: overdraft b/d 2,740, less undercast receipts 440, plus bank charges 150, dishonoured cheque 200 and the understated cheque 36 (62 - 26), gives an overdraft of 2,686. Bank reconciliation statement at 28 February 2006: overdraft per bank statement 1,600, add unpresented cheque 900 and the cheque wrongly charged to another account 1,100 (3,600), less the uncredited cheque 820 and the other customer's cheque charged in error 94, gives an overdraft of 2,686 per cash book.

Land and buildings 500,000 and 700,000; Motor vehicle 250,000 and 200,000; Stock 20,000 and 40,000; Debtors 12,000 and 35,000; Creditors 50,000 and 54,000; Bank 5,000 and (2,250) [overdrawn]; Cash 1,000 and 250; Drawings - (nil) and 12,000.

(b) Profit or Loss statement for the year ended 31st December, 2006,
(c) Balance Sheet as at that date.
questions.markingGuide:

4 marks: (a) Closing statement of affairs: assets N975,250 less creditors N54,000 and bank overdraft N2,250 = capital N919,000
4 marks: (b) Profit = closing capital 919,000 - opening capital 738,000 + drawings 12,000 = N193,000
3 marks: (c) Balance sheet: capital 738,000 + profit 193,000 - drawings 12,000 = N919,000, represented by fixed assets 900,000, current assets 75,250 less current liabilities 56,250
questions.explanation: Opening statement of affairs (1/1/2006): land and buildings 500,000, motor vehicle 250,000, stock 20,000, debtors 12,000, bank 5,000 and cash 1,000 total 788,000. Less creditors 50,000 gives capital 738,000. Closing statement (31/12/2006): assets 700,000 + 200,000 + 40,000 + 35,000 + 250 = 975,250. Less creditors 54,000 and bank overdraft 2,250 gives capital 919,000. Profit = 919,000 - 738,000 + 12,000 drawings = 193,000. Balance sheet: fixed assets 900,000; current assets 75,250 (stock 40,000, debtors 35,000, cash 250); current liabilities 56,250 (creditors 54,000, overdraft 2,250). Net assets 919,000 = capital 738,000 + profit 193,000 - drawings 12,000.

W. Roberts decided to purchase the business of Shade D. Forster on 1st May, 2005 when Shade D. Forster's balance sheet was as follows:
Balance Sheet as at 30th April, 2005: Capital D35,100; Current liabilities - Creditors D3,360; total D38,460. Fixed assets: Fixtures D1,920, Motor van D21,000 (D22,920); Current assets: Stock D5,160, Debtors D7,500, Bank D2,880 (D15,540); total D38,460.
W. Roberts was to take over all assets and liabilities of Shade D. Forster except cash at bank. Fixed Assets were revalued as follows: Fixtures D7,920; Motor van D20,000.
Additional information:
(a) 5% was to be provided for bad debts.
(b) W. Roberts was to pay a goodwill equal to three years' purchase of the average profit for the last five years. These were D4,290; D3,720; D5,040; D5,910 and D4,590.
(c) The transactions were duly carried out and payment was made to Shade D. Forster by cash.
You are required to:
(i) show the journal entries to record the above transactions;
(ii) prepare the Balance Sheet as at 1st May, 2005, after the transactions.
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Goodwill: average profit D4,710 x 3 = D14,130
2 marks: Provision for bad debts 5% of 7,500 = D375; net debtors D7,125
2 marks: Net assets taken over D36,845 (7,920 + 20,000 + 5,160 + 7,125 - 3,360); purchase consideration D50,975
4 marks: Journal: Dr Goodwill 14,130, Fixtures 7,920, Motor van 20,000, Stock 5,160, Debtors 7,500; Cr Provision for bad debts 375, Creditors 3,360, Vendor (Shade D. Forster) 50,975; then Dr Vendor 50,975, Cr Cash 50,975; with narrations
5 marks: Balance sheet at 1 May 2005: goodwill 14,130, fixtures 7,920, motor van 20,000, stock 5,160, debtors 7,125 (net); creditors 3,360; capital D50,975
questions.explanation: Goodwill = 3 x average profit (23,550 / 5 = 4,710) = 14,130. Net assets taken over: fixtures 7,920 + van 20,000 + stock 5,160 + debtors 7,125 (7,500 less 5% provision 375) - creditors 3,360 = 36,845. Purchase consideration = 36,845 + 14,130 = 50,975. Journal: debit Goodwill 14,130, Fixtures 7,920, Motor van 20,000, Stock 5,160 and Debtors 7,500; credit Provision for bad debts 375, Creditors 3,360 and Shade D. Forster (vendor) 50,975. Then debit Shade D. Forster 50,975 and credit Cash 50,975 for the payment. W. Roberts' balance sheet at 1 May 2005: fixed assets (goodwill 14,130, fixtures 7,920, van 20,000) 42,050; current assets (stock 5,160, debtors 7,125) 12,285; less creditors 3,360; net assets 50,975, financed by capital 50,975 (cash introduced to pay the vendor).

questions.explanation: (a) An income and expenditure account is prepared by clubs and societies and is their equivalent of a profit and loss account. It contains only revenue items. It is prepared on the accruals basis, so income and expenses are adjusted for amounts owing and prepaid. It includes non-cash items such as depreciation. Expenditure is on the debit side and income on the credit side. Its balance is a surplus or deficit, which is transferred to the accumulated fund. (b) Subscriptions in advance are paid by members before the period they relate to; they are a liability and are excluded from the year's income. Subscriptions in arrears are due for the period but unpaid; they are an asset and are included in the year's income.

questions.explanation: (a)(i) Liquidity ratios show whether a business can pay its short-term debts as they fall due, by relating current or liquid assets to current liabilities. (ii) Profitability ratios show how well a business earns profit, by relating profit to sales or to capital employed. (b) Liquidity: current ratio, and acid test (quick) ratio. Profitability: gross profit margin, net profit margin, and return on capital employed. (c) Ratios are used to compare a firm's performance over time and with other firms; to judge its liquidity and solvency; and to help management, investors and lenders in planning and decision-making.

questions.explanation: (a) A capital reserve is created from capital profits, i.e. profits that do not arise from normal trading, such as a share premium or a gain on revaluation. It is normally not available for distribution as dividend. (b) Share premium, revaluation reserve, capital redemption reserve, profit on reissue of forfeited shares, capital reserve on acquisition of a business, and pre-incorporation profit. (c) Revenue reserves are transferred from the profit and loss appropriation account (debit appropriation account, credit reserve account); capital reserves are credited directly from the capital transaction. In the balance sheet all reserves are shown under capital and reserves, as part of shareholders' funds.
